title: Ignatius of Antioch (c. 107)
hook: on his way to the lions he writes seven letters, the first to use the words the catholic church

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clement writes to Corinth: a letter for peace, and the noble one willing to step aside. Your line was peace in the church.

A prisoner is being marched across Asia toward Rome. He's chained to a squad of soldiers, and in one letter he calls them ten leopards, who only get worse the kinder he is to them. At the end of the road, wild beasts wait in the arena. Along the way, churches send people to meet him, sit with him, bring news. And whenever he can, the prisoner writes letters back. He's the bishop of Antioch, and his name is Ignatius.
screen: `A PRISONER ON THE ROAD TO ROME.` → `TEN LEOPARDS.` → `LETTERS FROM THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, where he comes from. Antioch is the city where, Acts says, the disciples were first called Christians. Ignatius leads that church as its bishop. In his letters' greetings he gives himself a second name: Theophorus, God-bearer. Second, the letter to Rome. The Christians there might have had friends with influence, people who could get a sentence changed. Ignatius begs them not to try. Don't be kind to me at the wrong time, he says; let me reach God. Then the line today's carry comes from: I am God's wheat, ground by the teeth of the beasts, so that I may be found pure bread of Christ. A bishop who has broken the bread of the Eucharist for his people now pictures his own body as grain for that bread. Third, a word still on church signs. To the Christians of Smyrna he writes: stay with your bishop, and just as wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the catholic church. Catholic is a Greek word meaning universal, whole. Ignatius uses it for the whole Church, gathered around Christ, wherever it is. Fourth, what worried him most. Some teachers said Jesus only seemed to have a body, only seemed to suffer. Ignatius pushes back again and again: Jesus was truly born, truly ate and drank, truly suffered and truly rose. For a man about to suffer in his own body, that mattered. His story is kept as a martyr's, not as a call to go looking for death, but as a picture of a life given away so completely that even its ending could become bread for others.
screen: `ANTIOCH, THEOPHORUS.` · `DON'T RESCUE ME.` · `WHERE CHRIST IS, THE CATHOLIC CHURCH.` · `TRULY BORN, TRULY SUFFERED.` · then, large: `I AM GOD'S WHEAT.`

segments.voice: Say his line to yourself on an out-breath: I am God's wheat. Then ask what is being ground in your life right now, a hard job, a long illness, a slow grief, and, without having to like it, what bread it might become, for you or someone else. If you pray, offer it to God; if not, let the picture of wheat and bread rest in you.
Theophorus. The name Ignatius gave himself, meaning God-bearer, as he wrote letters on the road to the beasts in Rome. Today's word.
Your line: wheat of God. Ground down, and still becoming bread. Day seven hundred three.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Ignatius of Antioch each year, name him in the Roman Canon of the Mass, and his letters appear in the Office of Readings.

original.note: Greek: the catholic church — katholikos means universal, whole. Ignatius, to the Smyrnaeans.

trapdoor: what you thought: catholic was a name the Church took much later.
what it means: the words the catholic church already appear in a letter Ignatius wrote on his way to die.

chat.says: Why did Ignatius call himself God's wheat?
options: Facing the beasts, he pictured his body ground like grain into pure bread of Christ.
Because he had farmed wheat near Antioch before the church made him its bishop.
Because as bishop he baked the bread for the Eucharist himself, every week.
chat.meaning: Ignatius wrote that he was God's wheat, ground by the teeth of the beasts to be found pure bread of Christ: a life given away completely.

Theophorus.meaning: God-bearer, the second name Ignatius gave himself

notes: 'I am God's wheat ... pure bread of Christ' (Romans 4) is paraphrased, not quoted, because the exact Lightfoot wording was not verified. A Keeper may wish to quote Lightfoot exactly.
'Don't be kind to me at the wrong time' paraphrases Romans 4 ('an unseasonable kindness'). 'Ten leopards' is Romans 5. Confirm.

Smyrnaeans 8 'catholic church': Lightfoot renders 'universal Church'. The index claims this is the first use of the words; the script does not make that claim (claims rule). Keeper may add it if a source is cited.
The index says 'seven letters'; the count is not in the letters themselves, so the script omits it. The seven-letter middle recension is the scholarly consensus; longer recensions exist.
Date 'c. 107' is the index's; Ignatius's date is debated. No date in the voice.
Ignatius in the Roman Canon and the Office of Readings: confirm.
